name: bkcrack
desc: Crack legacy zip encryption with Biham and Kocher's known plaintext attack
why: Implements the Biham and Kocher known-plaintext attack that cracks legacy zip encryption, a vivid lesson in how stream ciphers fail.

brief.what_it_is: bkcrack is a command-line tool that implements Biham and Kocher's known-plaintext attack against traditional PKWARE encryption (ZipCrypto) in ZIP archives. It takes a ciphertext entry plus 12 or more bytes of known plaintext, either from zip archives or plain files, and recovers the three 32-bit internal keys. From those keys it can decrypt the entry, strip or change the archive's password, or brute-force the original password.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a demonstration of a known weakness: legacy ZIP encryption can be broken with known plaintext, and the recovered internal state also decrypts other entries encrypted with the same password.
brief.how_it_works: The legacy cipher produces a keystream from a generator with three 32-bit state integers, initialized from the password and updated with the plaintext as encryption proceeds. Given ciphertext and at least 12 bytes of matching plaintext (at least 8 of them contiguous), the attack recovers that internal state. The README notes that more contiguous known plaintext makes the attack faster.

commands_seen.context: Lists entry names and metadata in a zip archive, showing which entries use ZipCrypto.
Loads ciphertext entry 'cipher' from encrypted.zip and known plaintext entry 'plain' from plain.zip, then runs the attack.
Runs the attack on raw files and saves the deciphered data to decipheredfile.
Deciphers data using internal keys already recovered in an earlier attack.
Writes a copy of the archive with no encryption, assuming all entries share the same password.
Writes a new archive encrypted with a password of your choice, using the recovered keys.
Brute-forces the original password from internal keys over printable ASCII characters.
Mask-based recovery for a password of 8 lowercase letters, a hyphen, and 6 digits; the README says this runs in milliseconds.
Supplies sparse known plaintext at specific offsets using -x, for when contiguous known bytes are too few.
Decompresses deflate-compressed deciphered data with the Python 3 helper script in the tools folder.
Configures the CMake build from source, with the install prefix set to the install folder.

brief.install_notes: Precompiled packages for Ubuntu, MacOS and Windows are on the GitHub releases page; extract the archive anywhere. On Windows the Microsoft Visual C++ Redistributable must be installed if it is not already present. To build from source, run cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=install, then cmake --build build --config Release, then cmake --build build --config Release --target install. Packages are also available from third-party repositories tracked on Repology. No accounts or configuration are mentioned.
brief.standout: It turns a well-known 1994 cryptanalysis into a usable tool that can remove or change an archive's password without knowing the password, using only the recovered internal keys. Its mask-based recovery, which the README says runs in milliseconds where brute force takes hours, makes the weakness concrete.
brief.status: maintained, with limited evidence. The README has CI, coverage, release and license badges and a releases link, and it describes a complete feature set. It gives no release date or last-commit date, and I did not check the releases or commit pages.
brief.caveats: It only works against legacy ZipCrypto entries, not AES-encrypted ZIPs, and it needs at least 12 bytes of known plaintext, with at least 8 contiguous. Deflate-compressed output needs a separate Python 3 script to decompress. On Windows it needs the Microsoft runtime. Brute-force cost grows as n^(l-6) for charset size n and password length l, so long passwords without a mask are impractical. License is zlib/png.
quotes: Crack legacy zip encryption with Biham and Kocher's known plaintext attack.
Given ciphertext and 12 or more bytes of the corresponding plaintext, the internal state of the keystream generator can be recovered.
This runs in milliseconds, whereas the bruteforce alternative takes hours.
